I noticed this when I walked **backwards**. It felt like my legs weren't really doing any pushing away from me, but rather that my body was leaning backwards and my legs were just bracing. Is forward and backward walking different because we only have toes in one direction?
Do humans walk by pulling with their legs or by leaning forward and merely bracing with the legs?

Walking, and to a greater extent, running, is basically controlled falling. It doesn't feel like falling because your trailing leg supports your weight for a lot longer than you may think, so the action is extremely smooth - when it comes to walking forward, anyway. You notice it a lot more when running - that's why having proper form is so important. You have to make sure your weight is being distributed in the least jarring way possible when you fall on to your leading foot.

You have to make sure your weight is being distributed in the least jarring way possible when you fall on to your leading foot.

Would you reckon this means that your body's vertical movement is as low as possible, or that the impact on your leading leg is as low as possible (by cushioning the blow with your foot as opposed to taking the brunt of the weight directly on your heel)?

It's more the latter than the former. I used the term jarring because it's as much about lessening your downward momentum as it is about absorbing the momentum you do have. Landing heel first is extremely jarring. You can feel it in your ankle, shin, knee, thigh and lower back. So the goal of running form is to make sure that the ball of your foot is hitting first, so your achilles tendon and calf muscle can absorb most of it, preserving the joints of your trailing leg, but more importantly, not wasting energy in stabilizing yourself.

I'm not an specialist; but I think when you're moving very slow, the movement of the legs individually are keeping your center of mass on top of your feet, but when walking normally, and running, it's more like how Segways (and the unfortunately named "hover"boards) work, were a torque is produced by the interaction with the ground is fighting gravity that would otherwise make you fall (because your center of mass isn't over your feet), resulting in an overall forward (or backward) motion. Though, at some walking speeds, I think you might actually be doing a hybrid of the two, keeping your center of mass directly supported only during part of each step, and falling forward during the rest.
